sanhedrin-4a-3-5.note: Students asked Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz about the verse on a woman who gives birth to a girl. Its letters, written without vowels, could be read as seventy days of impurity instead of two weeks. He answered with an argument: the Torah doubles the period of purity after a girl compared with a boy, so it must also double the impurity, from seven days to two weeks. After they left he went after them and said: you do not need that proof. We read it as two weeks, and the way the text is read is what counts.
sanhedrin-4a-3-5.why: Rabbi Yohanan has listed Sages who hold that the Torah's traditional reading, not its bare written letters, decides the law. This baraita is the Gemara's proof for Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz
people.about: A Sage whose students question him about a verse in Leviticus.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
In a state of ritual impurity, which bars a person from the Temple and from holy things for a set time.
The traditional pronunciation of the Torah's words, which the written text, having no vowels, does not show.

sanhedrin-5a-9-10.note: When Rabba bar Hana went down to Babylonia, his uncle Rabbi Hiyya asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: my brother's son is going down to Babylonia; may he teach? May he judge? May he declare firstborn animals permitted? To each the answer was yes. When Rav went down to Babylonia, Rabbi Hiyya asked the same about his sister's son. Rav was allowed to teach and to judge, but not to declare firstborn animals permitted.
sanhedrin-5a-9-10.why: The Gemara has been asking whether permission to judge given in the Land of Israel works in Babylonia, and now asks what that permission consists of. It goes on to ask why Rav was called a sister's son and refused one part.

people.name: Rabba bar Hana
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's brother's son, setting out for Babylonia.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Uncle of Rabba bar Hana and of Rav, who asks permission on their behalf.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; the one who grants permission to teach and judge.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's nephew, called his sister's son, also setting out for Babylonia.

terms.meaning: The male firstborn of a kosher animal belongs to the Temple and may not be eaten, but if it gets a permanent blemish it may be eaten. A Sage had to judge the blemish.
To judge money cases; with permission, a judge who erred was exempt from paying for his mistake.

sanhedrin-5b-5-7.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi came to a place where people were kneading dough while ritually impure, sure it would stay pure. They told him a visiting Torah scholar had taught that swamp water does not make food able to become impure, so they used it. He had actually taught that "water of eggs", egg white, does not, and they had misheard. They had also misunderstood a teaching that the swamp water of two rivers is unfit for the purification water of the red heifer, taking it to mean that this water did not count as water at all. At that time, the Sages decreed that a student may not teach unless his teacher gives him permission.
sanhedrin-5b-5-7.why: The Gemara asked why a scholar who knows the law would need permission merely to teach what is permitted and forbidden. This incident is its answer: a careless teacher can mislead a whole town.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; he discovers the town's mistake.

terms.meaning: Food can become ritually impure only after it has been wetted by water or certain other liquids.
Water mixed with the ashes of the red heifer to purify people from contact with the dead; it must be running water.

sanhedrin-5b-9-9.note: Rabbi Hiyya saw a man standing in a cemetery and asked him: are you not the son of a certain priest? Priests may not have contact with the dead. The man said yes, but explained that his father had been a man with "raised eyes" who set his eyes on a divorcee and married her, and so disqualified his son from the priesthood.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage surprised to see a priest's son in a cemetery.

terms.meaning: A man who wanted whatever he saw, even what was forbidden to him.
A priest is forbidden to marry a divorced woman; a son of such a marriage loses the status and duties of a priest.

sanhedrin-7b-5-6.note: The house of the Nasi appointed a judge who was not learned. The judge told Yehuda bar Nahmani, Reish Lakish's interpreter, to stand over him as interpreter while he lectured. Yehuda bar Nahmani bent over to listen, but the judge said nothing at all. So the interpreter began on his own with Habakkuk's verse: Woe to him who says to the wood, awake, to the dumb stone, arise; it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath in it. He added that God will one day punish those who appoint such judges.
sanhedrin-7b-5-6.why: The Gemara has been teaching that a judge must be independent and not seek gifts. Afterward Reish Lakish compares appointing an unfit judge to planting an idolatrous tree, and Rav Ashi reads "gods of silver and gold" as judges appointed for money.

people.name: Yehuda bar Nahmani
people.about: Reish Lakish's interpreter, told to serve the unlearned judge.

terms.meaning: The president of the Great Sanhedrin, the head of the Sages' court and of the Jewish community.
A man who stood beside a Sage during a public lecture and repeated and explained his words aloud to the audience.

sanhedrin-7b-18-18.note: Rav's host, with whom he sometimes stayed, came before him for a judgment. Rav asked: are you not my host? He said yes, and that he had a case to be judged. Rav told him he was disqualified from judging him, and told Rav Kahana to go out and judge it. Rav Kahana saw that the host was acting haughtily, and told him: if you will listen, listen; if not, I will take Rav out of your ears.
sanhedrin-7b-18-18.why: The Gemara is reading the verse "You shall not respect persons in judgment," which Rabbi Yehuda takes to mean a judge must not recognize a litigant as a friend. Rav's refusal to judge his own host puts that into practice.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who refuses to judge the case of a man who hosted him.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage Rav sends to judge the case instead.

terms.term: take Rav out of your ears
terms.meaning: Rav Kahana's warning that the host's tie to Rav would not help him in court.

sanhedrin-11a-0-1.note: Rabban Gamliel asked for seven Sages to come early to the upper room to intercalate the year, and in the morning he found eight. He said: whoever came up without permission must go down. Shmuel HaKatan stood and said it was he, and that he had come only to learn the practical law, not to take part. Rabban Gamliel told him: sit, my son, sit; every year would be fit to be intercalated by you, but the Sages said only those invited may do it. The Gemara adds that it was not really Shmuel HaKatan who had come uninvited but someone else; he spoke up to spare that person shame.
sanhedrin-11a-0-1.why: A baraita rules that the year may be intercalated only by those the Nasi invited, and this incident shows that rule in force. The Gemara then traces the habit of taking blame to spare another's shame back through Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, who summons seven Sages to intercalate the year.

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: A Sage who claims to be the uninvited eighth.

terms.meaning: To add an extra month to the year so that the lunar calendar stays in step with the seasons and Passover falls in spring. Only a court of Sages could decide it.
The president of the Great Sanhedrin, the head of the Sages' court and of the Jewish community.

sanhedrin-11a-2-2.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was teaching when he smelled garlic, and said: whoever ate garlic should leave. Rabbi Hiyya stood up and left, and then everyone stood up and left. The next morning Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son, found Rabbi Hiyya and asked: are you the one who upset my father? Rabbi Hiyya answered: such a thing should not happen among the Jewish people. He had not eaten garlic; he left so that whoever had would not be shamed.
sanhedrin-11a-2-2.why: The Gemara tells this as a parallel to Shmuel HaKatan claiming to be the uninvited Sage, and then asks where Rabbi Hiyya learned this conduct.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; the teacher who cannot bear the smell of garlic.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who walks out of the lecture.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who questions Rabbi Hiyya the next day.

sanhedrin-11a-3-3.note: A woman came to Rabbi Meir's study hall and said: Rabbi, one of you betrothed me through intercourse. Rabbi Meir got up, wrote her a bill of divorce and gave it to her. Then all the others got up, wrote bills of divorce and gave them to her, so the man was never singled out.
sanhedrin-11a-3-3.why: The Gemara asks where Rabbi Hiyya learned to take blame on himself to spare another's shame. This is its answer, and the chain then runs back to Shmuel HaKatan and Shecaniah ben Jehiel.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Head of the study hall, who writes the woman a bill of divorce first.

terms.meaning: One of the ways a man could make a woman legally his betrothed; she could not marry anyone else until he divorced her.
The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage or betrothal.

sanhedrin-11a-6-6.note: After the last prophets, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, died, the Divine Spirit left the Jewish people, but they still made use of a Divine Voice. Once the Sages were reclining in the upper room of the house of Gurya in Jericho, and a Divine Voice told them: there is one here fit for the Divine Presence to rest on him as on Moses, but his generation is not worthy. The Sages looked to Hillel the Elder. When he died they said of him: alas, the pious man, alas, the humble man, a disciple of Ezra.
sanhedrin-11a-6-6.why: The Gemara has just praised Shmuel HaKatan's piety; this story about Hillel opens a teaching of the Sages whose next part tells the same of Shmuel HaKatan.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: The Sage the others take to be the one the Divine Voice meant.

terms.meaning: The spirit of prophecy, which the text says left the Jewish people after the last prophets.
A voice from Heaven, described here as what the Sages still heard after prophecy ended.
God's presence resting on a person, as it rested on Moses in prophecy.

sanhedrin-11a-7-7.note: Another time the Sages were reclining in an upper room in Yavne, and a Divine Voice said: there is one here fit for the Divine Presence, but his generation is not worthy. The Sages looked to Shmuel HaKatan. When he died they said of him: alas, the pious man, alas, the humble man, a disciple of Hillel. As he was dying he said: Shimon and Yishmael to the sword, their companions to execution, the rest of the people to plunder, and great troubles will come upon the world. The Sages wanted to say the same of Yehuda ben Bava, but the hour was torn, for those executed by the government are not eulogized.
sanhedrin-11a-7-7.why: It completes a teaching that set Shmuel HaKatan beside Hillel the Elder, told because the Gemara had just praised Shmuel HaKatan for taking blame to spare another's shame.

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: The Sage the others take to be the one the Divine Voice meant; a disciple of Hillel.

people.name: Shimon
people.about: Named in Shmuel HaKatan's dying words as one who will die by the sword; the Nasi of the Great Sanhedrin.

people.name: Yishmael
people.about: Named with Shimon in Shmuel HaKatan's dying words; the High Priest.

people.name: Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: A Sage executed by the government, so the Sages could not eulogize him.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven, described here as what the Sages still heard after prophecy ended.
God's presence resting on a person, as it rested on Moses in prophecy.
The moment was lost: the Sages could not give him the eulogy they wanted.

sanhedrin-11a-9-9.note: Rabban Gamliel went to ask permission from a governor in Syria and was delayed in coming back. The Sages intercalated the year on condition that Rabban Gamliel would want it. When he returned and said, I want it, the year was found to be intercalated.
sanhedrin-11a-9-9.why: A baraita rules that the year may be intercalated only if the Nasi wants it. This incident shows how the court kept that rule while he was away, by making the extra month depend on his consent.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, away in Syria when the year needed to be intercalated.

terms.meaning: To add an extra month to the year so that the lunar calendar stays in step with the seasons and Passover falls in spring. Only a court of Sages could decide it.
The president of the Great Sanhedrin, the head of the Sages' court and of the Jewish community.

sanhedrin-11b-1-3.note: Rabban Gamliel sat on a step on the Temple Mount with Yohanan the scribe standing before him and three blank sheets of parchment ready. He dictated three letters. The first two told the people of the Galilee and of the South that the time had come to clear out tithes still in their possession, from the olive vats and from the stacks of grain. The third told the Jews of Babylonia, Media and the rest of the Diaspora that the young birds were still tender, the lambs thin and spring not yet come, so 'it seemed good to me and to my colleagues' to add thirty days to the year.
sanhedrin-11b-1-3.why: The Gemara contrasts the stern earlier leaders with the humble later ones, and this letter shows Rabban Gamliel adding thirty days. Because he mentions his colleagues, the Gemara suggests he wrote it after he had been deposed and had to share his office.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Leader of the Sages, who dictates the official letters

people.name: Yoḥanan
people.about: The scribe who stands before Rabban Gamliel and writes the letters

terms.meaning: The duty, at set points in the seven-year farming cycle, to hand over or remove tithes that were set aside from produce but never given to the people they belong to.

terms.term: Adding thirty days to the year
terms.meaning: Intercalation: inserting an extra month so the calendar of festivals stays in step with the spring season.

sanhedrin-12a-5-6.note: During a time of Roman persecution, the Sages of the Land of Israel sent Rava a message in code. A pair of scholars had set out from Rakkath and been seized by 'the eagle', the Roman soldiers, while carrying 'items made in Luz', which the Gemara explains was sky-blue dye. By divine mercy and their own merit they came out safely. The 'offspring of Nahshon' had wanted to 'establish a pillar', that is, add a month to the year, but 'that Edomite', the Roman governor, would not let them. Even so, the assembly gathered and established it in the month in which Aaron the priest died.
sanhedrin-12a-5-6.why: A teaching says the court may not add a month to the year before Rosh HaShana. The Gemara cites this message as a case where it was done in summer; it answers that the court may calculate early but may not announce it until after Rosh HaShana.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage in Babylonia to whom the coded message was sent

terms.meaning: A rare blue dye needed for the ritual fringes on a garment's corners; here it is smuggled goods the scholars were carrying.
Code for adding an extra month to the year, so that the festivals stay in their proper season.

terms.term: The month in which Aaron died
terms.meaning: Code for the summer month of Av, before the new year.

sanhedrin-13b-11-11.note: Rav says Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava should be remembered favorably: without him, the laws of fines would have ceased in Israel. The Roman government once decreed that anyone who ordained a judge would be killed, anyone ordained would be killed, the town where it happened destroyed and its boundaries uprooted. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava went out to a spot between two mountains and two towns, between Usha and Shefaram, and there ordained five elders, among them Rabbi Meir. When their enemies found them he told them, 'My sons, run.' They asked what would become of him; he said he lay before the Romans like a stone no one could overturn. The soldiers did not leave until they had driven three hundred iron spears into him, leaving him like a sieve.
sanhedrin-13b-11-11.why: A teaching says ordination needs three judges, and the Gemara asks whether one man could ordain. This story seems to show one man doing it; the Gemara replies that others may have been with him and were left unnamed out of respect for him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: An elderly Sage who ordained five students despite the Roman decree, and was killed for it

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: One of the five elders he ordained

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who says Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava should be remembered favorably

terms.meaning: The formal granting of the title Rabbi, giving a Sage authority to judge cases such as fines.
Penalties set by the Torah that only properly ordained judges could impose.
The limit around a town beyond which one may not walk on Shabbat; he sat between two such limits so that no town could be blamed.

sanhedrin-14a-7-7.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan kept trying to ordain Rabbi Ḥanina and Rabbi Hoshaya, but something always got in the way, and he was very upset about it. The two of them told him not to be upset: they were descended from the house of Eli.
sanhedrin-14a-7-7.why: The Gemara has been discussing who may be ordained and where. This story leads to Rabbi Yonatan's teaching, from the curse on Eli's house, that his descendants are never to be ordained.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A teacher who repeatedly tries and fails to ordain the two Sages

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: A Sage whom Rabbi Yoḥanan wanted to ordain

people.name: Rabbi Hoshaya
people.about: A Sage whom Rabbi Yoḥanan wanted to ordain

people.name: Eli
people.about: The High Priest from whom the two Sages say they descend

terms.meaning: The formal granting of the title Rabbi, which gives a Sage authority to judge.

sanhedrin-14a-9-10.note: Rabbi Zeira used to hide so that he would not be ordained, because Rabbi Elazar taught: stay obscure and stay alive. When he heard Rabbi Elazar's other teaching, that no one rises to greatness unless all his sins are forgiven, he presented himself for ordination. At his ordination the Sages sang him a wedding song for a bride: no eye shadow, no rouge, no hair dye, and still she is full of grace. When Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi were ordained, they sang: ordain for us anyone like these, but not the worthless or the twisters of the law (or, in another version, not robbers or bullies).
sanhedrin-14a-9-10.why: This is one of a run of ordination stories in the discussion. The songs sung at these ceremonies lead the Gemara on to the song the women of the emperor's house sang for Rabbi Abbahu.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who first avoided ordination, then sought it

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: The Sage whose two sayings changed Rabbi Zeira's mind

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: A Sage ordained together with Rabbi Asi

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: A Sage ordained together with Rabbi Ami

terms.meaning: The formal granting of the title Rabbi, which gives a Sage authority to judge.

sanhedrin-19a-9-9.note: At first, when people comforted mourners, the mourners stood in place and everyone else filed past them. But two families in Jerusalem kept fighting over this, each insisting, 'We pass first.' So the Sages decreed that the people should stand and the mourners should pass by them.
sanhedrin-19a-9-9.why: Rav Pappa has just learned from a teaching about the High Priest that mourners stand while the people pass. This teaching explains why that custom was once reversed; the Gemara then adds that Rabbi Yosei later restored it in Tzippori.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

sanhedrin-19a-15-16.note: A slave of King Yannai killed a man. Shimon ben Shataḥ told the Sages to put the king on trial. They sent word to Yannai, who sent them the slave; they replied that he must come too, since the Torah says the owner of an ox that kills must stand with his ox. Yannai came and sat down. Shimon ben Shataḥ told him to stand, for he stood before the One who spoke and the world came into being. Yannai said he would stand only if the other judges told him to. Shimon ben Shataḥ turned right and left, and the judges stared at the ground in silence. He said, 'You are masters of thoughts; may the Master of thoughts come and punish you.' At once the angel Gabriel struck them to the ground and they died. Then the Sages ruled that a king neither judges nor is judged.
sanhedrin-19a-15-16.why: The mishna says a king does not judge and is not judged, and Rav Yosef limits this to the kings of Israel, not the house of David. The Gemara asks why those kings are exempt and answers with this incident.

people.name: Yannai
people.about: The king whose slave killed a man, summoned to court

people.name: Shimon ben Shataḥ
people.about: The Sage who insists the king stand trial

people.name: Gabriel
people.about: The angel who strikes down the silent judges

sanhedrin-25a-9-10.note: A certain slaughterer was found to have sold meat from an animal that was not kosher. Rav Naḥman disqualified him as a witness and removed him from his post. The man went and let his fingernails and hair grow long, as a sign of remorse, and Rav Naḥman thought of reinstating him. Rava said to him: perhaps he is only putting on a show. The story does not say what Rav Naḥman decided.
sanhedrin-25a-9-10.why: The discussion is about who is disqualified as a witness. After Rava's doubt, the Gemara asks how such a man can prove he has changed, and answers with Rav Idi bar Avin's test: he must give up something valuable in a place where nobody knows him.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who removed the slaughterer and then considered reinstating him

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who suspects the man's repentance is a trick

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal injury or defect; its meat is forbidden even if it was slaughtered properly.
The trained person who kills animals in the ritual way, and whom buyers trust to sell only permitted meat.

sanhedrin-25b-23-23.note: Rabbi Zeira's father collected taxes for thirteen years. Whenever the chief tax collector of the region came to town, he warned the rabbis with a verse from Isaiah: 'Come, my people, enter your chambers.' To the townspeople he said that the chief collector was coming and would now slaughter father before son and son before father. Everyone hid, and when the chief arrived he asked him, 'From whom shall I collect?' On his deathbed he told those around him to take thirteen coins tied in his sheet and return them to a certain man: he had taken them from him and had not needed them.
sanhedrin-25b-23-23.why: Rav Yehuda has just ruled that an ordinary tax collector may serve as a witness unless he is known to collect more than people owe. This story shows a tax collector who protected his town and gave back money he took without need.

people.name: The father of Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A tax collector who shielded his town and returned money on his deathbed

terms.meaning: The chief tax collector over the region, who came to town to collect.
A small silver coin.

sanhedrin-26a-7-19.note: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Zarnokei and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak were travelling to Asya to add a month to the year, and Reish Lakish joined them to watch. Twice in the Sabbatical Year he saw a man working a field, once pruning vines and once plowing, and each time he exclaimed, 'A priest!' Each time the two offered an excuse for the man, and he rejected one of them: 'The heart knows whether it is for a bale or for deceit.' Calling him a nuisance, they climbed a roof and pulled the ladder away so he could not follow. Reish Lakish asked Rabbi Yoḥanan whether such men could set the calendar, calling them a conspiracy of the wicked; Rabbi Yoḥanan said this was troubling. When the two complained that Reish Lakish had called them cattle herders, he said 'shepherds' would not have been too harsh.
sanhedrin-26a-7-19.why: The Gemara has explained how heavy Roman taxes led the Sages to go easier on those who gather produce in the Sabbatical Year. Reish Lakish's phrase leads the Gemara to ask where the rule that a conspiracy of the wicked is not counted comes from.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage who joins the trip and objects to the travellers' leniency

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Zarnokei
people.about: One of the two Sages sent to add a month to the year

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
people.about: The other Sage sent to add a month to the year

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The teacher whom both sides come to

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when fields in the Land of Israel must lie fallow and may not be plowed or pruned.

terms.term: Adding a month to the year
terms.meaning: Intercalation: inserting an extra month so the festivals stay in their season; only qualified Sages could decide it.
The Gemara explains that priests were suspected of disregarding the Sabbatical Year, so Reish Lakish assumed the workers were priests.
Earlier the Gemara noted that cattle herders know nothing of law, and that ordinary shepherds may not serve as witnesses, so both were insults.

sanhedrin-26b-26-28.note: Some gravediggers buried a body on the first day of the festival of Shavuot. Rav Pappa excommunicated them and disqualified them as witnesses, but Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, declared them fit. Rav Pappa asked: aren't they wicked? Rav Huna answered that they thought they were doing a good deed. Rav Pappa asked: but I excommunicated them! Rav Huna answered that they thought the Sages were giving them atonement, not condemning them.
sanhedrin-26b-26-28.why: Rav Naḥman has just said that one who steals at harvest time is not called a thief and remains a valid witness. This case asks the same thing about people who broke the law believing they were doing right.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who excommunicated and disqualified the gravediggers

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage who declared the gravediggers fit to testify

terms.meaning: Placed under a ban that cut a person off from the community until he changed his ways.
A festival day on which, like Shabbat, most work is forbidden.
A commandment or good deed; burying the dead is a major one.

sanhedrin-27a-20-20.note: A man named bar Ḥama killed a person. The Exilarch told Rav Abba bar Ya'akov to investigate and, if bar Ḥama had certainly killed him, to have his eyes put out. Two witnesses testified that he had. Bar Ḥama brought two witnesses against one of them: one said he had seen him steal a measure of barley, the other a spear handle. Rav Abba bar Ya'akov objected that the law follows Rabbi Yosei, who lets a man caught out in money matters still testify in capital cases. Rav Pappi answered that this does not hold where an unnamed teaching follows Rabbi Meir, as one does here. The Gemara works out which teaching he meant. One witness was disqualified and bar Ḥama went free; he kissed Rav Pappi's feet and took on paying his tax for the rest of his life.
sanhedrin-27a-20-20.why: The Gemara has ruled that a witness who has done monetary wrong is disqualified even in capital cases, because an unnamed mishna follows Rabbi Meir. Asked where that mishna is, it answers with this case.

people.name: Bar Ḥama
people.about: A man accused of killing a person, who discredits a witness against him

people.name: The Exilarch
people.about: The head of the Babylonian Jewish community, who orders the investigation

people.name: Rav Abba bar Ya'akov
people.about: The Sage sent to investigate

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: The Sage whose argument gets bar Ḥama acquitted

terms.meaning: A teaching in the Mishna given without a Sage's name; the law usually follows it, so it can settle a dispute between named Sages.
A dry measure, a few liters.
Trials where the defendant's life or body is at stake, as opposed to cases about money.

sanhedrin-28a-31-31.note: Rav came to a certain place to buy parchment, and the people there asked him whether a man may testify about his stepson's wife. Two versions of his answer survive. In Sura they say he answered that a husband is like his wife, so the stepson's wife counts as the man's daughter-in-law. In Pumbedita they say he answered that a wife is like her husband, so she counts as his stepson; Rav Huna, quoting Rav Naḥman, finds this in the Torah's calling an uncle's wife 'your aunt'.
sanhedrin-28a-31-31.why: The discussion is listing which relatives by marriage may not testify about one another, case by case. This question adds one more such relationship.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who is asked the question while buying parchment

terms.meaning: Two Babylonian centres of learning; each preserves its own version of Rav's answer.

sanhedrin-28b-18-22.note: A deed of gift came before Rav Yosef signed by two witnesses who were brothers-in-law. He wanted to accept it, since Shmuel had ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yosei, whom he understood to allow brothers-in-law. Abaye asked how he knew Shmuel meant that version of Rabbi Yosei's view, and the two argued over what Shmuel meant when he said he and his brother Pineḥas could not testify together. Rav Yosef then told the holder to take possession through the witnesses who saw the deed handed over. When Abaye objected that even then a deed with invalid signatures is invalid, Rav Yosef told the man: go, the rabbis will not let me give it to you.
sanhedrin-28b-18-22.why: The discussion is about which in-laws may not serve as witnesses, and has just cited Shmuel's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Yosei. Rav Yosef tries to apply it, and Abaye shows that it is unclear which version of Rabbi Yosei's view Shmuel meant.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who first wanted to accept the deed and finally sent its holder away.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who challenged each of Rav Yosef's reasons.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage whose ruling on Rabbi Yosei is in question.

people.name: Pineḥas
people.about: Shmuel's brother, also his brother-in-law.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Early Sage whose view on brothers-in-law as witnesses is debated.

terms.meaning: A document recording that property was given as a gift, signed by two witnesses.
In Rabbi Elazar's view a document takes effect through the witnesses who see it handed over, not those who sign it.
Here, men married to two sisters.

sanhedrin-28b-27-27.note: Mar Ukva's brothers-in-law had been his relatives by marriage, but that tie had ended. When they came before him for judgment, he said he was disqualified from judging them. They asked whether he was following Rabbi Yehuda, and offered to bring a letter from the Land of Israel saying the law does not follow him. Mar Ukva answered, 'Am I stuck to you with a measure of wax?' He agreed they were no longer relatives; he was stepping aside only because they would not obey his verdict.
sanhedrin-28b-27-27.why: The Gemara has just reported rulings that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda, who says a former in-law with children from the marriage stays disqualified. Mar Ukva's case shows a judge who accepts this and still steps aside for another reason.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A judge who refuses to hear his former brothers-in-law's case

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel, seen from Babylonia.

terms.term: Stuck with a measure of wax
terms.meaning: An expression: do you think I am glued to you? He means he is no longer related to them.

sanhedrin-29b-7-9.note: A miser people called 'a mouse lying on dinars' said on his deathbed that certain men had money claims against him. After he died they sued his heirs. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, ruled that while a man may lie about debts during his life so as not to look rich, on his deathbed he is believed. The heirs paid half. When the claimants sued for the other half before Rabbi Ḥiyya, he said a man may also lie so that his sons will not look rich. The heirs asked to go back and undo the first payment; Rabbi Ḥiyya said, 'The elder has already ruled.'
sanhedrin-29b-7-9.why: Rav Naḥman has just ruled that a person's loose talk about owing money does not bind him, because people say such things so as not to look rich. This case asks whether that holds for words spoken on a deathbed.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The first judge, who holds the heirs liable

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: The second judge, who disagrees but will not overturn the elder's ruling

terms.meaning: Coins; the nickname mocks a man who sat on his money without using it.

sanhedrin-30b-1-5.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim had tried without success to get Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, ordained. One day Rabbi Yoḥanan asked his students whether anyone knew if the law follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa. Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim said his friend knew, and asked Rabbi Yoḥanan to ordain him first. Rabbi Yoḥanan did, then asked what he had heard. He said Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa agrees with Rabbi Natan. Disappointed, Rabbi Yoḥanan said, 'For this I needed him?' since it was obvious. Still he told him, 'Since you have gone up, you will not come down.' Rabbi Zeira concluded that once a great man is ordained, the ordination stands.
sanhedrin-30b-1-5.why: The discussion is whether two witnesses must see an event and testify together, a dispute between Rabbi Natan, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa and others. The story turns on that question, and the Gemara then gives Rav's ruling on it.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim
people.about: A Sage who manoeuvres to get his friend ordained

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: The Sage who is ordained and reports the teaching

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The teacher who ordains him and is let down by the answer

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: The Sage who draws a rule from the incident

terms.meaning: The formal granting of the title Rabbi, which gives a Sage authority to judge.
That two witnesses need not have seen the event together for their testimony to be combined.

sanhedrin-31a-10-10.note: A rumor spread about a certain student that he had revealed something said in confidence in the study hall, twenty-two years earlier. Rav Ami expelled him from the study hall, saying, 'This one is a revealer of secrets.'
sanhedrin-31a-10-10.why: A teaching forbids a judge to tell a litigant that he voted to acquit but was outvoted, citing the verse about a talebearer who reveals secrets. Rav Ami's act shows how seriously such disclosure was taken, even decades later.

people.name: Rav Ami
people.about: The Sage who expels the student

terms.meaning: The house of learning where the Sages discussed and taught Torah.

sanhedrin-31a-23-24.note: A child was brought to court before Rav Naḥman. Asked whether he had witnesses, he said no; asked whether he had any evidence, he said no; and Rav Naḥman ruled against him. As the child walked off crying, some people heard him and said, 'We know about your father's affairs.' Rav Naḥman ruled that in such a case even the Rabbis agree their testimony is accepted, since a child does not know his father's business.
sanhedrin-31a-23-24.why: The mishna says that if someone declared he had no witnesses and then produced some, they are worthless, and the law follows the Rabbis on this. Rav Naḥman's case marks the limit of that rule: it does not apply to a child.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who first rules against the child, then accepts his witnesses

terms.meaning: Here, the majority of Sages in the mishna, who say late witnesses are not accepted once a litigant has said he has none.

sanhedrin-31a-25-28.note: A woman was holding a promissory note on someone's behalf, and she said she knew it had been repaid. Rav Naḥman believed her. Rava asked whether this was because Rabbi held that handing over a note transfers ownership; Rav Naḥman said no, she was believed because she could have burned it. In another version Rav Naḥman did not believe her, and when Rava said she could have burned it, he answered that once a note has been confirmed in court that argument no longer works. Rava challenged him with a teaching that a receipt held by a trustee is valid. The Gemara concludes that Rav Naḥman's view is refuted.
sanhedrin-31a-25-28.why: It comes right after another of Rav Naḥman's rulings on whose testimony a court accepts, in the discussion of the mishna on new evidence after a verdict.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who rules on the woman's claim

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who questions and finally refutes Rav Naḥman

terms.meaning: A signed document recording a loan, which the lender can use to collect.
A note whose witnesses' signatures the court has verified, giving it full legal force.
A neutral third party who holds a document for two sides.

sanhedrin-33a-7-8.note: A cow from the household of Menahem had its womb removed. Rabbi Tarfon ruled that the injury would kill it and that it was forbidden as food, so the owner fed it to the dogs. Later the Sages at Yavne ruled such a cow permitted, because Theodosius the doctor reported that cows and pigs are never allowed out of Alexandria in Egypt until their wombs have been cut out. Rabbi Tarfon cried, "Your donkey is gone, Tarfon," expecting to have to pay for the cow. Rabbi Akiva told him he was exempt, because any judge accepted as an expert by the public does not have to pay for his mistakes.
sanhedrin-33a-7-8.why: Rav Sheshet has said a judge's ruling is revoked if he forgot an explicit teaching, but stands if he erred in weighing opinions. Rav Hamnuna raises this case against him: why did Rabbi Akiva not simply say Tarfon's ruling was void? The Gemara answers that Akiva gave both reasons.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: The Sage who ruled the cow forbidden and then feared he owed its owner the cost of it.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Tells Rabbi Tarfon he does not have to pay.

people.name: Theodosius the doctor
people.about: A physician whose report on the cattle of Alexandria led the Sages at Yavne to permit the cow.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: Raises this incident as an objection to Rav Sheshet.

terms.meaning: An animal with an injury or defect that will kill it within a year. Its meat is forbidden to eat even if it is slaughtered properly.
A town where the Sages held their court and study house.
A judge whom the community has accepted as qualified to rule. If he rules wrongly in good faith, he is not liable to pay for the loss.

sanhedrin-37a-7-7.note: Some hooligans lived in Rabbi Zeira's neighborhood. He treated them as friends so that they would repent, and the other Sages disapproved. When Rabbi Zeira died, the hooligans said: until now the short one with the singed legs prayed for compassion for us; who will pray for us now? They thought this over in their hearts and repented.
sanhedrin-37a-7-7.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rabbi Zeira's reading of a verse: even the traitors and sinners among the Jewish people carry some goodness. The story shows him living by that belief, and his hope for the sinners being borne out.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who befriended the hooligans next door so that they would repent, against the other Sages' wishes.

sanhedrin-37b-2-2.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Shatah swore that he once saw a man chase another man into a ruin. He ran after them and found the man holding a sword dripping with blood, with the victim convulsing on the ground. He said to him: Wicked man, who killed this man, you or I? But I cannot do anything to you, because the Torah requires two witnesses for a death sentence, and I did not see you kill him. The One Who knows thoughts will punish you. The Sages said that before they left the spot, a snake came and bit the killer, and he died.
sanhedrin-37b-2-2.why: A teaching has just said that a witness who saw only a chase, a bloody sword and a dying man has seen nothing and cannot testify to the murder. This case shows that rule at work. The Gemara then asks why a murderer would die from a snakebite.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: Sees a killer with a bloody sword over his victim but cannot have him put to death without two witnesses to the killing itself.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law. The Gemara often quotes one as evidence.

sanhedrin-38a-1-2.note: Yehuda and Hizkiyya, the young sons of Rabbi Hiyya, sat at a meal with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and said nothing. Rabbi told his servants to give them more wine so that they would talk. Once they were drunk, they said that the Messiah will not come until two families in Israel are destroyed: the family of the head of the exile in Babylonia, and the family of the Nasi in the Land of Israel, which was Rabbi's own. Rabbi said: My children, are you throwing thorns in my eyes? Their father, Rabbi Hiyya, asked him not to take offense. The word for wine and the word for secret both add up to seventy in Hebrew letters, he said: when wine goes in, secrets come out.

people.name: Yehuda
people.about: A son of Rabbi Hiyya who says, once drunk, what he had kept quiet about.

people.name: Hizkiyya
people.about: Yehuda's brother, also a son of Rabbi Hiyya.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi. He is the host of the meal and the Nasi whose family the young men name.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Father of Yehuda and Hizkiyya. He defends his sons to Rabbi.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel. The office passed down within one family.
The leader of the Jewish community in Babylonia, also called the Exilarch.
The Messiah, the future king descended from King David.

sanhedrin-39a-1-2.note: The Roman emperor told Rabban Gamliel that his God is a thief, because He put Adam to sleep and took one of his ribs. The emperor's daughter said she would answer. She asked her father for an officer, because bandits had come in the night, taken a silver jug and left a gold one. He said he wished such bandits would come every day. She said that this was just what happened to Adam: a rib was taken and he was given a wife to serve him. The emperor answered that God should have done it openly. She had raw meat brought, roasted it under the embers and offered it to him, and he said it disgusted him. So too, she said, Adam would have been disgusted by Eve if he had watched her being taken from him.
sanhedrin-39a-1-2.why: The Gemara is collecting replies to challenges against verses of the Torah. Just before this, a launderer answers a heretic on Rabbi Yishmael's behalf; here the emperor's daughter answers her father for Rabban Gamliel in the same way.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage the emperor challenges.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who calls God a thief.

people.name: the emperor's daughter
people.about: She answers her father's challenge for Rabban Gamliel.

sanhedrin-39a-4-5.note: The emperor told Rabban Gamliel that it was nothing great for God to count the stars, since he could count them too. Rabban Gamliel put quinces in a sieve, spun it and told him to count them. The emperor asked him to hold them still, and Rabban Gamliel said the sky turns in the same way. In another version, the emperor claimed to have counted the stars. Rabban Gamliel asked him how many teeth he had, and the emperor put his hand in his mouth to count them. Rabban Gamliel said: you do not know what is in your own mouth, and you know what is in the sky?
sanhedrin-39a-4-5.why: This is one in a run of exchanges between the emperor and Rabban Gamliel. Just before, the emperor claimed to know where God sits and was told he does not even know where his own son is.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who answers the emperor's boast.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who claims he can count the stars.

sanhedrin-39a-9-9.note: The emperor invited Rabbi Tanhum to make Jews and Romans into one people. Rabbi Tanhum agreed, but said that circumcised Jews could not become uncircumcised, so the Romans should be circumcised and become like them. The emperor said the argument was a good one, but anyone who defeats the king in argument is thrown to the wild animals. Rabbi Tanhum was thrown in and the animals did not eat him. A heretic said this was only because they were not hungry. Then the heretic was thrown in, and the animals ate him.
sanhedrin-39a-9-9.why: This belongs to a series of debates between Sages and a Roman emperor, heretics or a Persian priest about God and the Jewish people.

people.name: Rabbi Tanhum
people.about: The Sage who wins his argument with the emperor and survives the wild animals.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who proposes one people and then throws Rabbi Tanhum to the animals.

people.name: a certain heretic
people.about: Says the animals were not hungry, and is eaten by them himself.

terms.meaning: A pen holding wild animals. People thrown into it were meant to be killed by the animals.

sanhedrin-39a-10-10.note: The emperor mocked Rabban Gamliel: the Jews say the Divine Presence rests wherever ten of them gather, so how many Divine Presences are there? Rabban Gamliel called over the emperor's servant, struck him on the neck, and asked why he had let the sun into the emperor's house. The emperor said that the sun shines on the whole world. Rabban Gamliel answered that if the sun, only one of countless servants before God, shines on the whole world, then the Divine Presence of God certainly does.
sanhedrin-39a-10-10.why: This is another in the run of exchanges between the emperor and Rabban Gamliel and other Sages, each answering a challenge to Jewish belief about God.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who answers the emperor's mockery with the example of the sun.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who mocks the idea of the Divine Presence.

people.name: the emperor's servant
people.about: Struck by Rabban Gamliel to set up his answer.

terms.meaning: God's presence as it rests in a particular place or among people.

sanhedrin-43a-19-19.note: A teaching reports that on the eve of Passover they hung the corpse of Jesus the Nazarene. For forty days beforehand a crier went out announcing that he was going to be stoned for sorcery, for inciting people to worship idols and for leading the Jewish people astray, and calling on anyone who knew a reason to acquit him to come forward. No one found a reason to acquit him, so they stoned him and hung his corpse on Passover eve.
sanhedrin-43a-19-19.why: The mishna says a crier goes out only as the condemned man is led to execution. This teaching seems to contradict it, since here the crier went out forty days early. Ulla answers that Jesus was a special case: he had close ties to the government, so the court gave him every chance.

people.name: Jesus the Nazarene
people.about: Here, a man condemned for sorcery and leading the Jewish people astray. He was stoned and his corpse hung on Passover eve.

terms.meaning: An official who announced in public who was being executed and for what, so that anyone with evidence for the accused could come forward.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

sanhedrin-43a-21-25.note: A teaching says that Jesus the Nazarene had five disciples: Mattai, Nakai, Netzer, Buni and Toda. They were brought to trial one at a time. Each pleaded for his life with a verse that plays on his own name, and the judges answered each one with another verse on the same name, saying that he should be executed. The text does not say what then happened to them.
sanhedrin-43a-21-25.why: The Gemara has just discussed the trial of Jesus. It adds this second teaching about his disciples, and then Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi expounds the last verse quoted, about the thanks-offering.

people.name: Mattai
people.about: A disciple of Jesus who pleads with a verse containing the word matai, "when."

people.name: Nakai
people.about: A disciple who pleads with a verse about the innocent, naki.

people.name: Netzer
people.about: A disciple who pleads with a verse about a branch, netzer.

people.name: Buni
people.about: A disciple who pleads with a verse about a firstborn son, beni.

people.name: Toda
people.about: A disciple who pleads with a verse about thanksgiving, toda.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

sanhedrin-44b-10-10.note: A man was being taken out to be executed. He said: if I committed this sin, let my death not atone for any of my sins; if I did not, let it atone for all of them. The court and all Israel are clear, he said, but the witnesses will never be forgiven. When the Sages heard this, they said that he could not be brought back for retrial, because the sentence had already been passed. He would be executed, and the guilt for his death would hang around the necks of the witnesses.
sanhedrin-44b-10-10.why: The mishna has just ruled that a condemned man may not publicly declare himself innocent, so as not to cast blame on the court and the witnesses. The Gemara then asks why this case needed saying, and answers that he is executed even when the witnesses take back their testimony.

terms.meaning: Being cleared of sin before God. The Sages taught that a condemned man's death, together with his confession, atones for his sins.

sanhedrin-46a-11-11.note: In the days of Greek rule, a man rode a horse on the Sabbath. He was brought to court and stoned, not because he deserved it, but because the times required it. In another case, a man had intercourse with his wife in public under a fig tree. He was brought to court and flogged, again not because he deserved it, but because the times required it.
sanhedrin-46a-11-11.why: Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov has just taught that a court may impose lashes and death even where Torah law does not require them, as a fence to keep people from sin. These two cases are his examples.

terms.meaning: The Sages' phrase for an emergency measure. A court could punish more harshly than the law prescribes when people had grown lax in some area.
The period when Greek rulers governed the Land of Israel.

sanhedrin-52b-1-2.note: Imrata bat Talei, a priest's daughter, committed adultery. Rav Hama bar Toviyya surrounded her with bundles of branches and burned her. Rav Yosef said he made two mistakes. First, Rav Mattana had taught that burning is carried out with a wick of lead. Second, a teaching from the verse about coming before the priests and the judge says that capital cases may be judged only when priests serve in the Temple.
sanhedrin-52b-1-2.why: The Gemara is explaining how execution by burning is carried out. Right after this, it turns to the mishna's report of another priest's daughter burned with branches.

people.name: Imrata bat Talei
people.about: A priest's daughter who committed adultery and was burned.

people.name: Rav Hama bar Toviyya
people.about: The judge who had her burned with branches.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Says Rav Hama bar Toviyya made two mistakes.

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: His ruling that burning is done with a lead wick is cited against Rav Hama bar Toviyya.

terms.meaning: The method the Sages describe for execution by burning: molten lead poured down the throat, rather than burning the body in a fire.
The Torah singles out a priest's daughter who commits adultery for death by burning.

sanhedrin-52b-3-3.note: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok, reported a case of a priest's daughter who committed adultery and was put to death by actual burning. The Sages told him the court at that time was not expert in the law. Rav Yosef said that it was a court of Sadducees.
sanhedrin-52b-3-3.why: The discussion has just faulted Rav Hama bar Toviyya for burning a priest's daughter with branches. It now turns to the mishna's similar report, and Rav Yosef explains why a court would have done it that way.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Reports the burning of a priest's daughter to the Sages.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Says the court in that case was a court of Sadducees.

terms.meaning: A Jewish group that rejected the Sages' traditions and read the Torah literally. Here, they took the burning literally.
A passage of the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments.

sanhedrin-52b-4-4.note: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok, remembered riding on his father's shoulders as a child when a priest's daughter who had committed adultery was brought out, surrounded with bundles of branches and burned. The Sages told him that he had been a minor then, and that a minor's testimony cannot be used as proof.
sanhedrin-52b-4-4.why: In the mishna's version the Sages dismissed his report by saying the court was not expert. The Gemara asks how both versions can be right, answers that there were two separate incidents, and then works out which one he told first.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Remembers seeing a priest's daughter burned when he was a child on his father's shoulders.

terms.meaning: A child below the age of legal responsibility. The Sages did not accept a minor's testimony as proof.

sanhedrin-59b-22-22.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta was walking along a road when lions came at him, roaring. He quoted the verse, "The young lions roar after their prey, and seek their food from God." Two thighs of meat came down from heaven. The lions ate one and left the other. He took it to the study hall and asked whether it was kosher. The Sages told him that nothing non-kosher comes down from heaven.
sanhedrin-59b-22-22.why: The Gemara has claimed that Adam was not allowed to eat meat. When a teaching says angels roasted meat for him, the Gemara answers that this was meat from heaven. It then asks whether such meat exists, and this story is the proof that it does.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta
people.about: Meets roaring lions on the road and is given meat from heaven.

terms.meaning: The house of study where the Sages met to learn and to decide questions of Jewish law.
Permitted to eat under Jewish law.

sanhedrin-64a-9-9.note: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name a story about a gentile woman who was very ill. She vowed that if she recovered, she would worship every idol in the world. She recovered and did so. When she reached Peor, she asked its priests how it was worshipped. They told her: you eat spinach and drink beer, and then defecate before it. She said she would rather fall ill again than worship an idol that way.
sanhedrin-64a-9-9.why: Rav Yehuda draws the lesson right after: the Jewish people were not like her, and the verse says they attached themselves tightly to Ba'al-Peor. A teaching that follows reads the same verse the opposite way.

people.name: a certain gentile woman
people.about: Vows to worship every idol if she recovers, but refuses to worship Peor.

terms.meaning: Ba'al-Peor, an idol the Torah mentions. It was worshipped by defecating before it.

sanhedrin-64a-12-12.note: Sabbeta ben Alas, a Jew, rented out his donkey to a gentile woman. When she reached Peor, she asked him to wait while she went in. When she came out, he asked her to wait while he went in. She said: aren't you Jewish? He said: what do you care? He went in, defecated before the idol and wiped himself on its nose. The priests of Peor praised him, saying no one had ever worshipped it so well.
sanhedrin-64a-12-12.why: The ruling that follows says that one who defecates before Ba'al-Peor has worshipped it, even if he meant to insult it. This story shows how an insult can turn into worship.

people.name: Sabbeta ben Alas
people.about: A Jew who rents out his donkey to a gentile woman and tries to insult the idol Peor.

people.name: a certain gentile woman
people.about: Hires Sabbeta's donkey and goes to worship at Peor.

terms.meaning: Ba'al-Peor, an idol the Torah mentions. It was worshipped by defecating before it.

sanhedrin-64a-14-15.note: Rav Menashe was traveling to Bei Torta. People told him an idol stood there, so he picked up a stone and threw it at it. They told him it was Mercury, an idol worshipped by throwing stones. He said that the mishna makes a person liable only for throwing a stone as worship. He went to the study hall to ask. The Sages told him one is liable even when he means to stone it as an insult. He offered to go and take the stone back. They told him that both taking a stone away and adding one make a person liable, since each stone taken away leaves space for another.
sanhedrin-64a-14-15.why: The Gemara has just ruled that throwing a stone at Mercury counts as worship even if the thrower meant to insult it. Here a Sage learns that ruling the hard way.

people.name: Rav Menashe
people.about: A Sage who throws a stone at an idol to insult it, then asks the study hall whether he has sinned.

terms.meaning: A Roman idol worshipped by throwing stones onto a pile beside it.
A passage of the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, which the Sages quote and argue over.
The house of study where the Sages met to learn and to decide questions of Jewish law.

sanhedrin-65b-10-11.note: Turnus Rufus, the wicked Roman governor, asked Rabbi Akiva what makes the Sabbath different from other days. Rabbi Akiva asked him what makes him more important than other men. Turnus Rufus said it was because his master, the emperor, wished it. Rabbi Akiva answered that the Sabbath is special because his Master, God, wished it. Turnus Rufus then asked how anyone knows which day is really the Sabbath. Rabbi Akiva said there were three proofs: the Sabbatyon River, which is calm only on the Sabbath; a necromancer, whose dead do not rise on the Sabbath; and the grave of Turnus Rufus's own father, which gives off smoke all week but not on the Sabbath. Turnus Rufus said: you have demeaned him, shamed him and cursed him.
sanhedrin-65b-10-11.why: A teaching has just said that the dead raised by one kind of necromancer do not rise on the Sabbath. The Gemara adds that Turnus Rufus put this same question to Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Turnus Rufus
people.about: The Roman governor who challenges Rabbi Akiva about the Sabbath.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Answers Turnus Rufus and names his father's grave as proof.

terms.meaning: A river in Jewish legend that rages all week and rests on the Sabbath.
Someone who claims to call up the dead and ask them questions.
The place where the wicked are punished after death. Here, the smoke from the father's grave is a sign that he is being punished there.

sanhedrin-65b-16-16.note: Rava created a man and sent him to Rabbi Zeira. Rabbi Zeira spoke to him, but the man did not answer. Rabbi Zeira said to him: You were made by one of the Sages; return to your dust.
sanhedrin-65b-16-16.why: Rava has just taught that the righteous could create a world if they wished; the Gemara tells of his created man as evidence for that claim, and follows it with another such report.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who, according to the story, created a man

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: The Sage to whom Rava sent his creation; he sends it back to dust

terms.meaning: The translation's word for Rava's created man: a human figure made by a Sage, which here can move but cannot speak.

sanhedrin-67b-16-16.note: Rav told Rabbi Hiyya that he had seen an Arab slice a camel with a sword, beat a drum, and the camel stood up again. Rabbi Hiyya asked whether there had been blood and excrement on the ground afterward. Since there had not, he concluded it was only a trick on the eyes, not real sorcery.
sanhedrin-67b-16-16.why: The discussion is about what magicians and demons can and cannot really do; Rabbi Hiyya's question shows how to tell a mere illusion from real sorcery, a distinction the mishna under discussion uses to decide who is liable.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who reports what he saw an Arab do to a camel

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage Rav tells; he shows it was an illusion

terms.meaning: An illusion that only makes it look as if something happened, as opposed to real sorcery that actually changes things.

sanhedrin-67b-17-17.note: Ze'eiri came to Alexandria in Egypt and bought a donkey. When he went to give it water, the spell broke and the donkey turned into the plank of a bridge. The sellers refunded his money, telling him they would not have done so for anyone but Ze'eiri, since everyone there tests a purchase with water before buying.
sanhedrin-67b-17-17.why: It is one of a string of tales about sorcery and illusion told while the Gemara discusses what magicians can really do.

people.name: Ze'eiri
people.about: A Sage who bought a bewitched donkey in Alexandria; the sellers refund him because of who he is

sanhedrin-67b-18-18.note: Yannai came to an inn and asked for water. He was brought a drink of flour and water, and he saw the innkeeper woman's lips moving. He spilled a little of it and it turned into scorpions. He said: I drank from yours, now you drink from mine. He gave her a drink and she turned into a donkey; he rode her to the marketplace. Her friend came and broke the spell, and people saw him riding on a woman in the marketplace.
sanhedrin-67b-18-18.why: It is one of a string of sorcery tales the Gemara tells while discussing what magicians can and cannot really do.

people.name: Yannai
people.about: A man who uncovered a spell on his drink and turned the innkeeper woman into a donkey

people.name: the innkeeper woman
people.about: She put a spell on Yannai's drink and was turned into a donkey

sanhedrin-68a-0-9.note: When Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues came to visit. It was Friday, and when his son Hyrcanus came to remove his phylacteries, Rabbi Eliezer scolded him for neglecting the serious Sabbath preparations. Seeing his mind was clear, the Sages sat four cubits away from him. He rebuked them for not coming to learn sooner, predicted they would not die a natural death and Rabbi Akiva's would be worse, and mourned the Torah dying with him, including the magic of planting cucumbers that only Akiva had asked him about. He answered their questions on ritual purity and died saying the word pure. Rabbi Yehoshua declared his ban lifted. After the Sabbath, Rabbi Akiva met the funeral, beat his flesh until it bled, and cried: I have many coins and no money changer.
sanhedrin-68a-0-9.why: The mishna says Rabbi Akiva learned about magically gathering cucumbers from Rabbi Yehoshua; the Gemara asks how, since this account shows he learned it from Rabbi Eliezer. It answers that he learned it from Eliezer but understood it only from Yehoshua.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A sick and dying Sage, under a ban, visited by his students

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's student, the only one who asked him about planting cucumbers

people.name: Hyrcanus
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's son, scolded for removing his phylacteries

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage present at the death who declares the ban lifted

terms.meaning: Tefillin: small leather boxes holding Torah verses, worn during weekday prayers but not on the Sabbath.
Rabbi Eliezer had been placed under a ban by the Sages, so people had to keep four cubits, about two meters, away from him.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first great written collection of Jewish law.
Rabbi Yehoshua's declaration that the ban on Rabbi Eliezer is lifted now that he has died.

sanhedrin-72a-13-13.note: Burglars broke into Rava's house and stole his rams. Later they came to return them, but Rava refused to take them back, saying: Since this ruling came from Rav's mouth.
sanhedrin-72a-13-13.why: The Gemara is discussing Rav's ruling that a burglar who could lawfully be killed takes ownership of what he stole; Rava's refusal shows that he acted on Rav's ruling himself.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage whose rams were stolen by burglars; he refuses to take them back

people.name: Rav
people.about: An earlier Sage whose ruling Rava cites

terms.meaning: Thieves who tunnel or break into a house; the Torah allows the homeowner to kill such a burglar, which affects whether the burglar must return what he took.

sanhedrin-75a-1-1.note: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that a man set his eyes on a woman and became so lovesick he was near death. Doctors said he would be cured only if she slept with him. The Sages said: Let him die rather than that. The doctors asked that she at least stand naked before him, then that she at least talk with him behind a fence. Each time the Sages said: Let him die.
sanhedrin-75a-1-1.why: The Gemara has been discussing when a person must die rather than transgress, including forbidden sexual relations; this case extends that to even small acts of intimacy, and the Gemara then debates whether the woman was married.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports the incident in Rav's name

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage in whose name the incident is told

sanhedrin-82a-4-5.note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Avuya taught that the skull of King Jehoiakim bore the words: This and yet another. The grandfather of Rabbi Perida found a skull lying at the gates of Jerusalem with those words on it. He buried it twice and twice it came back up, so he knew it was Jehoiakim's. Saying a king should not be disgraced, he wrapped it in silk and put it in a chest. His wife found it, and the neighbors told her it must be the skull of his first wife whom he could not forget. She heated the oven and burned it. When he came home he said: This is what was written on it, This and yet another.
sanhedrin-82a-4-5.why: It follows another teaching of Rabbi Hiyya bar Avuya in the discussion about relations with gentile women; the Gemara gathers a second saying of his and the story that bears it out.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Avuya
people.about: Sage who taught about the writing on Jehoiakim's skull

people.name: Rabbi Perida
people.about: His grandfather found the skull

people.name: Jehoiakim
people.about: A king of Judea whose skull is found unburied at Jerusalem's gates

sanhedrin-90b-20-20.note: The Roman emperor challenged Rabban Gamliel: You say the dead will live, but they become dust, and can dust come to life? The emperor's daughter said: Leave him, I will answer him. She asked her father which of two craftsmen is greater, one who shapes vessels from water or one who shapes them from clay. He said the one who works with water. She answered: If he can shape from water, surely he can shape from clay.
sanhedrin-90b-20-20.why: The discussion is gathering arguments for the resurrection of the dead; the daughter's parable joins Rabbi Meir's answer to Cleopatra and the reasoning from glass vessels that follows.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A Sage challenged by the emperor about resurrection

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who doubts that dust can live again

people.name: the emperor's daughter
people.about: She answers her father with a parable about two craftsmen

terms.meaning: The belief that God will bring the dead back to life in the future.

sanhedrin-91a-5-8.note: The people of Afrikiya came before Alexander of Macedon claiming the land of Canaan, since the Torah calls it the land of Canaan and Canaan was their ancestor. Geviha ben Pesisa asked the Sages for permission to argue: if he lost, they could say only a simple man had lost; if he won, the Torah of Moses had won. He cited the Torah's curse that Canaan would be a slave to his brothers: a slave's property belongs to his master, and they owed years of unpaid service besides. Alexander told them to answer. They asked for three days, found no answer, and fled, leaving their fields sown and vineyards planted. It was a Sabbatical Year.
sanhedrin-91a-5-8.why: The Gemara has just told of Geviha ben Pesisa's sharp reply to a heretic about resurrection; it now brings his debates on behalf of the Jewish people, recorded as the reason for a holiday on the 24th of Nisan.

people.name: Geviha ben Pesisa
people.about: A Jew who argues the Jewish people's case before Alexander

people.name: Alexander of Macedon
people.about: The king who hears the dispute

people.name: Canaan
people.about: The ancestor the people of Afrikiya claim, cursed in the Torah to be a slave

terms.meaning: An ancient list of joyous dates on which fasting was forbidden, each marking a past deliverance.
Every seventh year, when Jews in the Land of Israel may not farm; the abandoned crops were a gift to them that year.

sanhedrin-91a-9-12.note: The Egyptians came before Alexander of Macedon demanding back the silver and gold the Israelites had borrowed when they left Egypt. Geviha ben Pesisa got the Sages' permission to argue the case. He cited the Torah's verse that Israel lived in Egypt for 430 years and demanded wages for 600,000 people enslaved all that time. Alexander told the Egyptians to answer; they asked for three days, found no answer, and fled, leaving their fields sown and vineyards planted. It was a Sabbatical Year.
sanhedrin-91a-9-12.why: It is the second of three debates in which Geviha ben Pesisa defends the Jewish people before Alexander, told after his reply to a heretic about resurrection.

people.name: Geviha ben Pesisa
people.about: A Jew who argues the Jewish people's case before Alexander

people.name: Alexander of Macedon
people.about: The king who hears the Egyptians' claim

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when Jews in the Land of Israel may not farm.

sanhedrin-91a-13-14.note: The descendants of Ishmael and of Keturah took the Jewish people to judgment before Alexander of Macedon, claiming a share of the land of Canaan, since the Torah calls both Ishmael and Isaac sons of Abraham. Geviha ben Pesisa asked the Sages' leave to argue: if he lost, they could say only an ordinary man was beaten; if he won, that the Torah of Moses had won. He asked his opponents for their proof; they said: the Torah. He answered from the Torah: Abraham gave all he had to Isaac, gave gifts to his concubines' sons and sent them away. A son sent away by a father who divided his property in his lifetime has no claim on the other. The outcome is not told here.
sanhedrin-91a-13-14.why: This is one of a series of cases in which Geviha ben Pesisa argued for the Jews before Alexander; just before, he answered the Egyptians' claim by demanding wages for the years of slavery in Egypt.

people.name: Geviha ben Pesisa
people.about: Argues for the Jewish people before Alexander, with the Sages' permission.

people.name: Alexander of Macedon
people.about: The ruler before whom the case is brought.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: Sage who explains what Abraham's gifts to the concubines' sons were.

terms.meaning: A wife of Abraham; her sons were among those he sent away with gifts.
A deed by which a father divides his property among his sons during his lifetime.

sanhedrin-93b-7-7.note: Bar Koziva ruled for two and a half years and told the Sages: I am the Messiah. They answered that the Messiah is said to judge by smell, and they would see whether he could. When they saw he could not, they killed him.
sanhedrin-93b-7-7.why: Rava has just read Isaiah's verse to mean the Messiah will judge by smell; the story puts that test to a man who claimed to be the Messiah.

people.name: Bar Koziva
people.about: A man who ruled two and a half years and claimed to be the Messiah

terms.meaning: The Gemara's reading of Isaiah 11:3, that the Messiah will sense who is right without relying on what he sees or hears.

sanhedrin-97a-5-6.note: Rava used to think there was no truth anywhere in the world, until Rav Tavut, a Sage who would not lie for all the world's wealth, told him this. He once came to a place called Truth, where no one lied and no one died before their time. He married a woman there and had two sons. One day his wife was washing her hair when a neighbor knocked; thinking it improper to say she was bathing, he said she was not there. His two sons died. The townspeople asked what had happened, and when he told them, they begged him to leave so he would not bring early death upon them.
sanhedrin-97a-5-6.why: A teaching has just said that before the Messiah comes truth will be lacking; this story, about the one place where truth lived, is told on that theme.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who reports Rav Tavut's account

people.name: Rav Tavut
people.about: A scrupulously honest Sage, also called Rav Tavyomei, who tells of the town of Truth

sanhedrin-97b-2-2.note: Rav Hanan bar Tahlifa sent word to Rav Yosef that he had met a man holding a scroll in Hebrew script and language. The man said he had served as a hired soldier in the Roman army and found it in the Roman archives. The scroll said that 4,291 years after creation the world would end, with the wars of the sea monsters, the wars of Gog and Magog, and the days of the Messiah, and that God would renew the world only after seven thousand years. Rav Aha, son of Rava, said the text read five thousand.
sanhedrin-97b-2-2.why: The Gemara is weighing traditions about when the Messiah will come; this scroll gives a date, and the discussion goes on to warn against calculating the end.

people.name: Rav Hanan bar Tahlifa
people.about: A Sage who reports finding the scroll

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage to whom he sends the report

people.name: Rav Aha, son of Rava
people.about: A Sage who gives a different number for the text

terms.meaning: The square Hebrew script used for Torah scrolls.
Names from the prophet Ezekiel for the enemies in a great war expected at the end of days.

sanhedrin-98a-14-16.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi found Elijah the prophet at the entrance to Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's tomb and asked if he would reach the World-to-Come; Elijah answered, If this Master wishes. He asked when the Messiah would come; Elijah told him to go ask him, at the gate of Rome, sitting among the sick poor, unbinding and rebinding one bandage at a time so he will be ready. Rabbi Yehoshua greeted him, and the Messiah greeted him back and said he would come today. When he did not come, Rabbi Yehoshua told Elijah the Messiah had lied. Elijah said he had meant: today, if you will listen to his voice.
sanhedrin-98a-14-16.why: The Gemara has been reading verses that say the redemption can come early if Israel merits it; the Messiah's 'today, if you listen' makes the same point in a story.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: A Sage who meets Elijah and then the Messiah

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who answers Rabbi Yehoshua's questions

people.name: the Messiah
people.about: Sits among the sick poor at Rome's gate and promises to come today

terms.meaning: The life of reward after this world, in Jewish tradition.

sanhedrin-98a-17-20.note: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma's students asked when the Messiah would come. He hesitated, fearing they would ask for a sign; they promised not to. He said: when this gate falls and is rebuilt, falls and is rebuilt, and falls again, and before it can be rebuilt the son of David will come. They then asked for a sign anyway, and he said the water of the Cave of Pamyas would turn to blood, and it did. As he was dying he told them to bury his coffin deep, because every palm tree in Babylonia would have a Persian horse tied to it and every coffin in the Land of Israel would become a feed trough for Median horses.
sanhedrin-98a-17-20.why: It is one of several teachings about the signs and timing of the Messiah's coming in this part of the discussion.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma
people.about: A Sage whose students ask him when the Messiah will come

terms.meaning: A name for the Messiah, who is to descend from King David.
A cave at a spring in the north of the Land of Israel, whose water he says will turn to blood.

sanhedrin-100a-3-3.note: Levi bar Shmuel and Rav Huna bar Hiyya were mending the cloth covers for the scrolls in Rav Yehuda's school. When they came to the scroll of Esther, they said this one does not need a cover. Rav Yehuda told them that talking this way also looks like irreverence.
sanhedrin-100a-3-3.why: The mishna lists the epikoros among those who lose the World-to-Come, and the Gemara is collecting examples of what counts as such disrespect; this remark about the scroll of Esther is one.

people.name: Levi bar Shmuel
people.about: One of two Sages mending scroll covers

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hiyya
people.about: The other Sage mending scroll covers

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Head of the school, who rebukes them

terms.meaning: Someone who treats Torah and its Sages with contempt; the mishna says such a person has no share in the World-to-Come.
Cloth covers wrapped around sacred scrolls as a mark of respect.

sanhedrin-100a-7-7.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan taught that God will one day set gems thirty cubits square, with openings bored through them, as the gates of Jerusalem. A student mocked him: we cannot even find a gem the size of a dove's egg. Later, at sea, the student saw ministering angels cutting such stones, and they told him they were for the gates of Jerusalem. Back home he told Rabbi Yoḥanan: teach, master, it is fitting for you to teach; I saw just what you said. Rabbi Yoḥanan answered: good-for-nothing, had you not seen it, you would not have believed? You mock the words of the Sages. He set his eyes on him and turned him into a pile of bones.
sanhedrin-100a-7-7.why: Rabbi Yirmeya asked whether an elder's praise of a Sage's teaching was disrespect. Rabbi Zeira says no, it was support; real disrespect is this student's, who agreed with Rabbi Yoḥanan only once he had seen it for himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Sage whose teaching about the gates of Jerusalem the student mocked.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Tells this story in answer to Rabbi Yirmeya's question.

terms.meaning: The angels who serve God.
An ancient measure of length, roughly the length of a forearm.

sanhedrin-101a-8-8.note: Rav Yitzhak bar Shmuel bar Marta stopped at an inn, and they brought him oil in a vessel. He rubbed it on his face, and boils broke out on it. When he went out to the marketplace, a woman saw him and said she could see the evil spirit of Hamat on his face. She performed an action for him, which the translation explains as whispering an incantation, and he was healed.
