sanhedrin-101a-8-8.why: A teaching just before warns that one may not smear oil brought in a vessel, since someone may have whispered a spell over it and it will harm him. This incident shows that exact danger.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Shmuel bar Marta
people.about: A Sage who rubbed oil from a vessel on his face at an inn and broke out in boils.

people.name: a certain woman
people.about: A woman in the marketplace who recognized the spirit on his face and cured him.

terms.meaning: The name of the evil spirit the woman said she saw on his face; the text treats the boils as its work.
Saying an incantation over oil. Oil whispered over could heal, or, as here, harm the person who used it.

sanhedrin-101a-10-16.note: When Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, his students came to visit. He said there was fierce wrath in the world. They wept; Rabbi Akiva laughed. As long as his teacher's wine, flax, oil and honey never spoiled, Akiva said, he feared Rabbi Eliezer had already received all his reward; now, seeing him suffer, he was glad. Asked whether he had neglected any of the Torah, Akiva quoted his teacher's own lesson: no one on earth is so righteous that he never sins. In a second account, four Sages visit. Three praise him as better for Israel than rain, the sun, or parents; Akiva says suffering is precious. Rabbi Eliezer asks to be propped up to hear, and Akiva proves it from King Manasseh, whom only suffering turned back to God.
sanhedrin-101a-10-16.why: Just before, a verse is read to say that even when God brings illness, He heals. These visits to the sick Rabbi Eliezer turn to the value of suffering, and the discussion then follows Manasseh's repentance.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Sage who fell ill and was visited by his students and colleagues.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's student, who laughed at his illness and taught that suffering is precious.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: Visitor who called Rabbi Eliezer better for Israel than rain.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Visitor who called Rabbi Eliezer better for Israel than the sun.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Visitor who called Rabbi Eliezer better for Israel than a father and mother.

terms.meaning: Got his whole reward in this life, leaving none for the World-to-Come.
The life after this one, where the righteous are rewarded.

sanhedrin-102a-17-17.note: Rabbi Abbahu used to lecture at length about the three wicked kings who, according to the mishna, have no share in the World-to-Come. When he fell ill, he took it upon himself to stop lecturing about them. Once he recovered, he lectured about them again. His students asked whether he had not promised to stop. He answered: did they repent, that I should take back what I said?
sanhedrin-102a-17-17.why: The Gemara is going through the mishna's list of kings with no share in the World-to-Come and has just spoken of Jeroboam's refusal to repent. Rabbi Abbahu's answer turns on that same point: the kings never repented.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage who used to lecture about the three wicked kings, stopped while he was ill, and started again when he recovered.

terms.meaning: Jeroboam, Ahab and Manasseh, kings of ancient Israel and Judah whom the mishna names as having no share in the World-to-Come.
The life after this one, in which the righteous have a share.
The first written collection of Jewish law. The Gemara is the discussion built around it.

sanhedrin-102b-1-3.note: Rav Ashi stopped his lecture just before the three wicked kings and told his students that tomorrow they would begin with 'our colleagues'. That night King Manasseh appeared to him in a dream, angry: you call us your colleagues? He asked Rav Ashi where one should begin cutting the bread when saying the blessing over it. Rav Ashi did not know. Asked to teach him, Manasseh said: from where the loaf is crusted from baking. Rav Ashi asked why, if he was so wise, he had worshipped idols. Manasseh said that had Rav Ashi been there, he would have lifted the hem of his cloak and run after him. The next day Rav Ashi told the Sages they would begin with 'our teachers'.
sanhedrin-102b-1-3.why: The Gemara is discussing the three kings the mishna says have no share in the World-to-Come. Rabbi Abbahu, just before, refused to soften his lectures on them; here Rav Ashi learns to speak of them with respect even while they stay condemned.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who called the three wicked kings his colleagues and was rebuked in a dream.

people.name: Manasseh
people.about: A wicked king of Judah, one of the three kings, who appears to Rav Ashi in a dream.

terms.meaning: The opening words of the blessing said over bread before eating it; the question is where to begin cutting the loaf for it.
Jeroboam, Ahab and Manasseh, kings whom the mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, names as having no share in the World-to-Come.

sanhedrin-104a-8-8.note: The Gemara asks why the wicked king Jehoiakim is not on the list of kings with no share in the World-to-Come, and answers with a report that 'This and yet another' was written on his skull. Rabbi Perida's grandfather found a skull lying at the gates of Jerusalem with those words on it. He buried it, and it would not stay buried; he buried it again, and again it came up. He decided it was Jehoiakim's skull, since the prophet said he would be buried like a donkey and cast out. Because it was a king's, he would not treat it with contempt: he wrapped it in silk and put it in a box. His wife saw it, thought it was the skull of his first wife that he could not forget, lit the oven and burned it. That, the text says, is what 'This and yet another' meant.
sanhedrin-104a-8-8.why: The Gemara is asking why certain wicked kings were left off the mishna's list of those with no share in the World-to-Come. This story is its answer for Jehoiakim: his skull suffered a further disgrace.

people.name: Jehoiakim
people.about: A wicked king of Judah; the skull with the writing on it is said to be his.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya, son of Rabbi Avuya
people.about: The Sage who reports the writing on Jehoiakim's skull.

people.name: Rabbi Perida's grandfather
people.about: The man who found the skull, tried to bury it, and kept it in a box.

people.name: his wife
people.about: The grandfather's wife, who thought the skull was his first wife's and burned it in the oven.

terms.meaning: The words written on the skull. The story reads them as a second disgrace after the first: first it would not stay buried, then it was burned.
The early Sages of the Mishna; here, the ones who drew up the list of kings with no share in the World-to-Come.

sanhedrin-104a-15-15.note: Two Jews were taken captive on Mount Carmel, and their captor walked behind them. One said to the other that the camel ahead of them was blind in one eye, carried two skins, one of wine and one of oil, and was led by two men, one a Jew and one a gentile. The captor called them a stiff-necked people and asked how they could know. They explained: the camel ate grass only on one side; wine drips and sinks into the ground while oil drips and floats; and the gentile relieved himself on the road while the Jew went off to the side. The captor ran ahead and found it all true. He kissed them on the head, brought them home, made them a great feast, danced before them, blessed the God who chose Abraham's descendants and gave them His wisdom, and set them free.
sanhedrin-104a-15-15.why: The Gemara has just read 'princess among the provinces' to mean that wherever the exiled Jews go, they become princes to their masters through their wisdom. The captor's own blessing repeats that phrase.

people.name: two captives
people.about: Two Jews taken captive on Mount Carmel who work out everything about a camel they cannot see.

people.name: the captor
people.about: The man holding them captive; he checks their claims, honors them and frees them.

terms.meaning: A phrase from the Bible for a stubborn people; the captor uses it as an insult when he thinks they are inventing things.

sanhedrin-104b-12-13.note: The Gemara asks who drew up the list of people with no share in the World-to-Come. Rav Ashi says the members of the Great Assembly did. Rav, quoted by Rav Yehuda, says they wanted to add one more, King Solomon. An image of his father, King David, came and threw itself down before them, and they paid it no heed. Fire came from heaven and scorched their benches, and they paid it no heed. A heavenly voice praised Solomon for building God's House before his own, and faster, and they paid it no heed. Then a heavenly voice said: shall the reward be as you wish? It is God, not they, who chooses.
sanhedrin-104b-12-13.why: The mishna has just listed kings and others who have no share in the World-to-Come, and the Gemara has been discussing them one by one. This story explains who made the list and why Solomon is not on it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who says the Great Assembly drew up the list.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who passes on Rav's account of the attempt to add Solomon.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who tells that the Great Assembly wanted to add Solomon to the list.

people.name: Solomon
people.about: King, son of David; the Great Assembly wanted to count him among those with no share in the World-to-Come.

people.name: David
people.about: Solomon's father; an image of him comes and prostrates itself to plead for his son.

terms.meaning: A body of sages and leaders after the return from the Babylonian exile, remembered for setting much of Jewish tradition.
A voice from heaven that announces God's will; in Hebrew, bat kol.
The life after this one, in which the righteous have a share.

sanhedrin-105b-8-8.note: A heretic who lived near Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi kept upsetting him. One day Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi took a rooster, tied it by its legs to a bed, and sat watching it, planning to curse the man at the exact moment of God's anger. When the moment came, he dozed off. He took this as a sign that it is not proper to curse, quoting the verse 'Punishment, even for the righteous, is not good', and concluded that one should not curse even heretics.
sanhedrin-105b-8-8.why: The Gemara has just said that God is angry for one moment each day, during the first three hours, and that the moment shows when the rooster's crest is white with no red streaks. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi tries to use that moment against his neighbor.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: A Sage who planned to curse a troublesome neighbor at the moment of God's anger and fell asleep instead.

people.name: a certain heretic
people.about: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's neighbor, who kept upsetting him.

terms.meaning: Here, a person who rejected the Sages' teachings and challenged them; in Hebrew, min.
Used here as a clock: the Gemara says the moment of God's anger can be told by the color of the rooster's crest.

sanhedrin-107b-11-13.note: When King Yannai was killing the Sages, Yehoshua ben Perahya and his student Jesus fled to Alexandria in Egypt. When peace came, Shimon ben Shatah called him home. At an inn on the way they were treated with great honor. Yehoshua ben Perahya praised the inn; Jesus remarked that the innkeeper's wife had narrow eyes. Yehoshua called him wicked for looking at a married woman, and ostracized him with four hundred shofar blasts. Jesus asked many times to be taken back, and was ignored. Once, during the Shema, Yehoshua meant to accept him and signaled with his hand to wait; Jesus thought he was being driven away, set up a brick and bowed to it. Told to repent, he said he had learned that one who sins and leads many to sin is not given the chance.
sanhedrin-107b-11-13.why: The Gemara has just told how Elisha drove Gehazi away. This is the next case of a teacher rejecting a student outright, and right after it comes the teaching to push away with the left hand while drawing near with the right.

people.name: Yehoshua ben Perahya
people.about: A Sage who fled to Alexandria with his student and later ostracized him.

people.name: Jesus
people.about: Yehoshua ben Perahya's student; ostracized, he turned to idol worship.

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: The Sage who wrote calling Yehoshua ben Perahya back to Jerusalem.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: A king who killed the Sages, which is why Yehoshua ben Perahya fled.

terms.meaning: Put under a ban, cut off from the community; here announced with four hundred blasts of the shofar.
Ram's horns blown as trumpets; here blown to announce the ban.
The central daily prayer declaring God's oneness ('Hear, O Israel'); one does not stop in the middle of it to speak.

sanhedrin-108b-21-21.note: Nahum of Gam Zo answered everything that happened to him with 'This too is for the best'. The Jews wanted to send a gift to the emperor and sent it with him, known for miracles. At a lodging on the way he said he was carrying tax for the emperor. At night the residents they emptied his chest and filled it with dirt. The emperor, finding dirt, said the Jews were mocking him, and Nahum was taken out to be killed. He said: this too is for the best. Elijah came, looking like one of them, and suggested it might be the dust of Abraham, which became swords when thrown. Thrown at a province they could not conquer, it won the battle. Nahum was let into the treasury and filled his chest with gold. The residents of the lodging then brought dirt to the emperor too, and they were executed.
sanhedrin-108b-21-21.why: Just before, Eliezer tells Shem how Abraham's thrown dust became swords and his straw became arrows. The Gemara follows with this story about that same dust.

people.name: Nahum of Gam Zo
people.about: A man who said 'This too is for the best' about everything; he carried the Jews' gift to the emperor.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who appears disguised as one of the emperor's men and saves Nahum.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who received the chest and was about to kill Nahum.

people.name: the residents of the lodging
people.about: People who stole the gift, filled the chest with dirt, and were later executed.

terms.meaning: Hebrew for 'this too', from Nahum's saying; it is also given as a place name.
A tradition, told just before this story, that when Abraham fought the kings, the dust he threw became swords and the straw became arrows.

sanhedrin-109a-15-15.note: Rabbi Yosei taught in Tzippori about the ways the people of Sodom stole. That night three hundred tunnels were dug into houses in Tzippori. The homeowners came and harassed him, saying he had shown thieves the way. He answered: did I know that thieves would come? When Rabbi Yosei died, the gutters of Tzippori ran with blood.
sanhedrin-109a-15-15.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rava's teaching that the people of Sodom used balsam to sniff out where homeowners kept their treasure and then dug in to take it. Rabbi Yosei's lecture on these methods leads to the tunnels.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who taught in Tzippori about how the people of Sodom stole.

terms.meaning: A town in the Galilee where Rabbi Yosei taught.
The biblical city destroyed for its wickedness; the Gemara here describes its people's cruelty and theft.

sanhedrin-110a-16-16.note: Rabba bar bar Hana tells that once, on a journey, an Arab offered to show him the place where Korah's followers had been swallowed. He saw two cracks in the ground with smoke coming out. The Arab dampened a woolen fleece with water, put it on the tip of his spear and passed it over the cracks, and it was singed. He told Rabba bar bar Hana to listen, and he heard voices saying: Moses and his Torah are truth, and we are liars. The Arab told him that every thirty days Gehenna turns them back to this spot, like meat in a cauldron, and they say this again.
sanhedrin-110a-16-16.why: The Gemara is reading the verses about Korah's rebellion against Moses, how the earth swallowed his followers and how Moses asked for the opening of Gehenna to be brought near. It has just cited a teaching that Korah's sons sang praise from a place in Gehenna.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage who tells of being shown where Korah's followers were swallowed.

people.name: a certain Arab
people.about: A guide who shows Rabba bar bar Hana the smoking cracks.

people.name: Korah
people.about: Led a rebellion against Moses in the wilderness; the earth swallowed his followers.

terms.meaning: The place where the wicked are punished after death.

terms.term: Moses and his Torah are truth
terms.meaning: What the swallowed rebels cry out: they now admit Moses was right and they were wrong.

sanhedrin-111a-6-6.note: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Yosei, tells that he once came to Alexandria in Egypt and met an old man, who offered to show him what his ancestors, the Egyptians, had done to Rabbi Elazar's ancestors. Some they drowned in the sea, some they killed with the sword, and some they crushed into the buildings.
sanhedrin-111a-6-6.why: The baraita adds that Moses was punished over this, for protesting to God that He had not saved His people. The Gemara then gives God's rebuke of Moses for questioning Him, when the forefathers never did.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who tells of his visit to Alexandria.

people.name: one old man
people.about: An Egyptian in Alexandria who shows him what the Egyptians did to the Israelites.

people.name: Moses
people.about: The text says he was punished for protesting to God over the Israelites' suffering.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

sanhedrin-68a-6-6.note: On his deathbed, Rabbi Eliezer recalls a walk with his student Akiva. Akiva asked him to teach him about planting cucumbers. Rabbi Eliezer said one statement, and the whole field filled with cucumbers. Akiva asked to be taught how to uproot them; Rabbi Eliezer said one statement, and they all gathered into one place.
sanhedrin-68a-6-6.why: The mishna mentions gathering cucumbers by sorcery as Rabbi Akiva's teaching; this memory shows where Akiva first learned it, and the Gemara goes on to ask how Rabbi Eliezer was allowed to perform magic at all.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A dying Sage who tells this memory of teaching his student

people.name: Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's student, who asked to learn the planting and uprooting of cucumbers
